AUTHORED.sub: IRS §7216 disclosure, shown before any document is uploaded

AUTHORED.detail: US law forbids disclosing return information without written consent naming who receives it. taxBuddy names exactly two companies — which is why the AI provider default is a compliance control.

AUTHORED.title: Eligibility
AUTHORED.sub: The five-year rule — and the residency test that is not implemented

group.note: The rule that is implemented, the one that is not, and the form that proves it.

AUTHORED.detail: Form 1040-NR is only correct for a nonresident, so the whole product rests on this gate — and the IRS's actual residency test is not in the codebase.

children.title: Five-Year Rule
children.sub: EXEMPT_YEAR_LIMIT = 5, and the gate compares with > not >=
children.detail: An F-1 student is an 'exempt individual' — exempt from counting days toward residency — for five calendar years. In year six they are a resident, and this product no longer applies.

rows.title: Count the exempt years
rows.detail: countedExemptYears filters the status grid for years carrying a non-empty letter, and counts the keys.

under.why: A count of KEYS, not a span of dates. Someone present Jan-Feb of five years and someone present for five continuous years produce the same number — the rule is defined in calendar years, so that is correct, and it is also why no date arithmetic appears anywhere near it.

rows.title: Compare against the limit
rows.detail: exemptYearsUsed > EXEMPT_YEAR_LIMIT blocks. Strictly greater, so exactly 5 passes and 6 blocks.

rows.label: 4 years used
rows.value: Passes — still exempt

rows.label: 5 years used
rows.value: Passes. The gate is >, not >=

rows.label: 6 years used
rows.value: Blocked — resident for tax purposes, wrong form

rows.title: Zero years fails CLOSED
rows.detail: An empty answer means the input never arrived, not that the filer was never a student. Counting zero would pass everyone.

under.why: The distinction between 'no' and 'no answer'. Because the grid always seeds the current tax year, a genuine zero is impossible — so zero can only mean the data is missing, and the safe reading of missing data on a gate is refusal.

rows.title: One writer of 'blocked'
rows.detail: app/api/eligibility/route.ts:87 is the only place in the repo that writes stage 'blocked'.

children.title: Substantial Presence
children.sub: The IRS residency formula is absent from the codebase

group.note: Two rewrites and a source, each answering a different question.

children.detail: The IRS test is a weighted three-year sum — this year's days, a third of last year's, a sixth of the year before, 183 or more means resident. That formula is not in this repository.
children.evidence: grep: no 1/3, no 1/6, no weighted sum in lib/rules/

anatomy.caption: what the IRS asks for vs. what the code does

rows.to: days(Y) + days(Y-1)/3 + days(Y-2)/6 ≥ 183 → resident

under.caption: what was searched for, and what 183 actually is here

rows.to: no * (1/3), no / 3 near 'prior', no 0.3333, no 0.16666, no 'weighted' anywhere in lib/rules or lib/audit
present — but as a DIFFERENT rule that happens to share it

under.why: The only 183 in the codebase, and it is the capital-gains presence threshold, not residency. Two unrelated tax rules share a number — which is exactly how a reader could convince themselves substantial presence is implemented when it is not.

rows.to: the five-year exempt-individual rule alone — and refuses everyone it doesn't cover

rows.title: Why the omission is survivable
rows.detail: An F-1 inside five years is exempt from counting days at all, so substantial presence never applies to anyone the gate admits.

rows.title: The gate refuses rather than tests
rows.detail: Every filer the five-year rule cannot answer for is turned away with a reason, not evaluated.

under.why: Each refusal names its own reason in the filer's words and every one says "yet". The chain is a scope boundary written as a conversation — which is why the missing formula costs nobody a wrong return: they are turned away before it would be needed.

rows.title: Deliberate or unfinished?
rows.detail: Not determinable from the repository. Nothing records which, and the two look identical from the outside.

children.title: Form 8843
children.sub: The form that proves the exemption the gate relies on

group.note: Form lines, each fed from a different fact.

children.detail: Every exempt individual files this, income or not. Lines 11 and 12 are the five-year rule on paper, and line 12 uses the gate's own count so the two cannot contradict.

rows.to: visa class held during the tax year
the exempt years themselves, listed
"were you exempt for more than 5 years?" — computed, never asserted

under.why: The same expression as the gate, reused rather than restated. A hardcoded "no" would be correct today and silently wrong the day the gate widens — this cannot drift because there is only one copy of the rule.

AUTHORED.title: Interview
AUTHORED.sub: The upload wizard: five stages ordered to hide each parse

group.note: The stage order, then three separate defects in the upload machinery.

AUTHORED.detail: Every upload step is followed by questions that don't depend on it, so the parse runs while the filer types. The wizard's order is a performance decision in a config file.

children.title: Stage Order
children.sub: Five stages, each one hiding the previous stage's parse latency

rows.title: eligibility
rows.detail: Documents plus questions that don't depend on them.

rows.title: confirm
rows.detail: Needs the I-94/I-20 read, which step 1 awaits on Continue — so this never spins. Last place a filer can be rejected.

rows.title: interview
rows.detail: The slowest parse in the app: a consolidated broker 1099 runs many pages. Which is why profile FOLLOWS it rather than precedes it.

rows.to: 1099 questions first — the longest parse starts earliest
1042-S next
W-2 last of the document questions
need no document at all — pure runway while the 1099 finishes

rows.title: profile
rows.detail: The longest form in the product, deliberately placed where it hides the income parse.

under.why: The clearest statement of the product's core performance trick. It also warns that the order is load-bearing: moving a step changes how long filers stare at a spinner, and five hand-stamped stage strings in API routes have to move with it.

rows.title: payout
rows.detail: The first screen that can state a refund, and the only place bank details are collected.

rows.label: Phases vs steps
rows.value: 4 phases over 5 steps — eligibility is split across two routes with nothing on screen saying so

rows.label: Checked at module load

rows.label: Why not a test

children.title: Upload Queue
children.sub: Module-level state that outlives every component that reads it

group.note: Three independent behaviours of the same module-level registry.

children.detail: Uploads are fire-and-forget. A module-level registry tracks what is in flight so a later step can ask 'may I advance yet', scoped to the JS context because a reload kills the fetches too.

rows.to: answers "may I advance yet" — synchronously

rows.label: hasPendingIncomeExtractions()
rows.value: Synchronous read of inFlight > 0

rows.label: Why synchronous matters
rows.value: It decides whether the processing screen appears AT ALL — asked after an await, it paints for one frame on every filing

rows.label: settleIncomeExtractions()
rows.value: Resolves immediately at zero, else parks a resolver until the count drains

rows.to: answers "what is the filer waiting on"

rows.label: Replaced, never mutated
rows.value: So useSyncExternalStore can compare snapshots by identity

rows.label: Rows stay after settling
rows.value: The screen checks them off rather than vanishing them

rows.label: Why co-located
rows.value: They are the same event — two modules would drift the moment one missed a settle

rows.to: aborts the fetch — or un-persists it if the abort lost the race

rows.title: Call every canceller for that docType
rows.detail: Reaches the AbortControllers held in the upload slot, which may already be unmounted — hence the module-level registry.

rows.title: Drop the named rows
rows.detail: Or the processing screen keeps listing a document the filer just disclaimed.

rows.title: Leave the COUNT alone
rows.detail: An aborted fetch still rejects, which still runs settle, which still decrements. Decrementing here too would double-count.

under.why: The division of labour is the subtle part: cancel touches cancellers and rows, never the counter. Leak the count and settleIncomeExtractions hangs forever, which the filer sees as a processing screen that never finishes.

rows.title: If it already committed
rows.detail: The emptied entries list makes the read's own 'removed while I was reading' branch fire — it deletes the income from the server rather than leaving it behind.

children.title: Cancel Race
children.sub: A guard that read false exactly when it needed to be true
children.detail: Answer yes, drop a W-2, change to no before the parse lands. The clear was gated on data having already arrived — false in exactly that window, so the read committed wages the filer had disclaimed.

rows.title: The bug, as the file describes it
rows.detail: The guard `w2s.length > 0` is false while the document is still being read — so nothing was cleared and nothing was cancelled.

under.why: A guard that looked like defensive programming WAS the bug. The consequence is the worst kind: a silently wrong tax return — invisible on screen, real on line 1a. The fix was deleting the condition, not strengthening it.

rows.title: Cancel first, then clear
rows.detail: Reversed, the clear lands and the still-running read puts the income straight back.

under.why: Three lines whose ORDER is the fix. The void is deliberate fire-and-forget — the interview must not block on a save, because the payout gate re-reads the server later and is the real safety net.

rows.title: Three handlers, identical shape
rows.detail: W-2, 1042-S and the four 1099 arrays each cancel their own docType. Keyed so de-selecting one income type cannot cancel another's read.

children.title: Lost Update
children.sub: Two documents finishing together, one stale snapshot written

group.note: Two snapshot reads that race; neither precedes the other.

children.detail: Each upload computed [...items, extracted] from the state captured when it started. Two dropped together meant the second save erased the first, after it was extracted and paid for.

rows.to: one commit at a time — fixes ORDERING

rows.label: Shape
rows.value: chain.current.then(work, work) — same handler for both outcomes

rows.label: Why both
rows.value: A rejected commit must not stall the queue behind it

rows.label: What the caller gets
rows.value: The real promise; the chain keeps a neutralized .catch copy

rows.to: each commit sees the last one's write — fixes STALENESS

under.why: Two orthogonal failure modes needing two mechanisms. The last two sentences exist to pre-empt the obvious future 'simplification' of dropping either half — and the endpoint replaces the whole array, so the client owns this correctness entirely.

AUTHORED.title: Extraction
AUTHORED.sub: A PDF becomes typed numbers — three model reads, one arbiter
AUTHORED.detail: BDA turns a PDF into markdown; three model legs read it into typed fields and are compared. Disagreements are supposed to be logged — the ledger reports zero rows against fourteen filings.

children.title: BDA Parse
children.sub: Hand-signed SigV4, S3 staging, and a pointer inside a pointer
children.summary: 9 steps: stage, sign, invoke, poll, then two pointer hops
children.detail: No SDK for this. 306 lines sign their own AWS requests, stage the PDF in S3, poll, then follow a pointer inside a pointer to the output.

rows.title: Stage the PDF in S3
rows.detail: Written to staging/input/{runId}.pdf. BDA reads from a bucket, never from a request body.

rows.label: Input key
rows.value: staging/input/{runId}.pdf

rows.label: Output prefix
rows.value: staging/output/{runId}/

rows.label: Deleted after?
rows.value: Attempted — and the failure path is a console.warn, not a throw

rows.title: Sign the request by hand
rows.detail: SigV4 over a JSON-1.1 target header. The signing service is 'bedrock' — not the endpoint's own name, which is the trap.

under.why: An AWS API called without an AWS SDK. Everything is manual: the target header names the operation, the path is always "/", and the body is JSON-1.1 — an RPC protocol wearing HTTP's clothes.

rows.title: Invoke, then poll
rows.detail: InvokeDataAutomationAsync returns an invocation ARN. The poll schedule is front-loaded: 4s, then 1s, 1s, 1s, widening to 3s.

rows.title: Follow the pointer to the pointer
rows.detail: The job result names a metadata file; that file names the standard output path. Two hops before any markdown exists.

under.why: Four levels of optional chaining to reach a filename. The fallback chain markdown → text → empty means a page BDA could not represent silently becomes an empty string rather than an error — which is exactly the failure the three-leg comparison downstream exists to catch.

rows.title: No retries at this layer
rows.detail: A failed BDA job throws. Whatever called it decides what to do — the parser itself never tries twice.

rows.label: Project ARN
rows.value: AWS's public default project — not one this account created

rows.label: Profile ARN
rows.value: Constructed from account and region rather than configured

rows.label: The Coral trap
rows.value: An error can arrive as HTTP 200 with an error body, so status alone is not success

rows.label: Staged PDF deletion
rows.value: 403s in production and logs a warning naming the PII left behind — per docs/STATUS.md

children.title: Three Legs
children.sub: Two models read the markdown, one reads the raw PDF

group.note: Three legs run concurrently — no leg waits for another.

shape.note: A and B share BDA's markdown; only C sees the PDF

children.detail: The same document read three independent ways. Agreement is evidence; disagreement is the signal that a parser dropped something.

rows.to: haiku-4-5 over BDA's markdown — the canonical leg
minimax-m2.5 over the same markdown — a different model, same text
haiku over the raw PDF — skips the parser entirely

rows.label: Why a third leg
rows.value: A and B share BDA's markdown, so they share its mistakes. C is the only leg that can catch the PARSER being wrong

rows.label: What it costs
rows.value: Reading a PDF directly is the most expensive of the three

rows.label: Canonical by default
rows.value: bda, unless EXTRACTION_CANONICAL_LEG says pdf-direct

rows.to: a measured failure: LlamaParse put a date 11 months wrong, silently

rows.label: Measured over
rows.value: 65 documents

rows.label: What happened
rows.value: A travel row was silently dropped and a residency date landed 11 months wrong

rows.label: Why it wasn't caught
rows.value: Every downstream check still passed — the value was well-formed, just wrong

rows.label: The lesson encoded
rows.value: A single reader cannot detect its own omission. Only disagreement can

children.title: Extraction Specs
children.sub: A dual schema whose field descriptions ARE the prompt

group.note: Two schema halves, read together rather than in turn.

children.detail: Each document type has a hand-written JSON Schema whose field descriptions the model reads, plus a Zod schema re-validating the reply. Nothing generates either from the other.

anatomy.caption: the arrangement, and the hazard in it

rows.to: carries the prose the model actually reads

under.code:
"COMPLETENESS — READ TO THE END OF THE DOCUMENT: the table often " +
            "breaks across pages, and the final row(s) frequently do not stay in " +
            "the table. After a page break they can appear as loose lines or " +
            "headings, one value per line, in the order row-number / date / type / " +
            "location (e.g. \"9\", \"2021-09-16\", \"Arrival\", \"SEA\"). Those are " +
            "travel-history rows and must be included, appended in row-number " +
            "order after the rows from the table. If the table ends at row 8 and a " +
            "stray \"9\" block follows, there are 9 rows, not 8 — the stranded row " +
            "is usually the earliest arrival, which is the row that determines the " +
            "residency start date."
under.why: This is the prompt, and it is a field description. It encodes a specific observed failure — a page break stranding the earliest arrival — and says why that row matters more than the others: it sets the residency start date, which decides the whole return.

rows.to: re-validates the reply on the way out
neither is generated from the other — they drift by hand

rows.label: Specs maintained
rows.value: 8 document types, each with both schemas

rows.label: Generation between them
rows.value: None. Adding a field means editing two places

rows.label: What drift looks like
rows.value: A field the model is told to return but Zod rejects — or one Zod expects that the model was never asked for

children.title: Resolution Ladder
children.sub: Arithmetic footing check, then a re-read off a second text layer
children.detail: Each read is first checked against itself: do the parts sum to the total? If not, a different text extractor gets a turn.

rows.title: Does it foot?
rows.detail: Arithmetic footing on the fields that should sum. A statement whose parts don't add up was read wrong.

rows.title: Re-read with pdftotext
rows.detail: A layout-preserving text layer, spawned as a process with the PDF on stdin.

under.why: A Node API footgun with a tax consequence. The wrong call produces empty output that looks exactly like a legitimately scanned document — so the bug masquerades as a correct diagnosis, on every file, forever.

rows.title: Guard on digits
rows.detail: A page with fewer than two digits is not a usable text layer, whatever it returned.

children.title: Disagreement Log
children.sub: Built, wired, migrated — and reporting zero rows

group.note: The write path and the read path of a ledger with no rows.

children.detail: Disagreements are meant to be written to a table for review. Five nested swallows mean a broken writer and a genuinely quiet extractor look identical.

rows.label: Rows today
rows.value: 0, against 14 filings — per docs/STATUS.md

rows.label: Swallowed exceptions
rows.value: 5 nested try/catch around the write

rows.label: What that means
rows.value: A broken writer and a genuinely quiet extractor produce identical observable behaviour

rows.label: Identifiers
rows.value: Redacted before writing — the ledger stores field paths, not values

rows.label: Reads
rows.value: Stored in extraction_disagreements

rows.to: a regex per document type — only these fields can disagree

under.code:
const TAX_LINE: Record<ExtractionKind, RegExp> = {
  w2: /^(box1|box2|box3|box4|box5|box6|box15State|box17StateTaxWithheld|box19LocalIncomeTax)$/,
  i94: /^(firstEntryDate|visaClass|citizenship|dob|legalName|travelHistory\.)/,

under.why: The comparison is scoped to fields that actually reach a tax line. It bounds the noise — but it also bounds what the ledger can ever notice, so a field outside these patterns can disagree freely and silently.

children.title: Provider Default
children.sub: Two stale comments describe a posture the code dropped

group.note: Two comments and the constant that contradicts them.

children.detail: Unset AI_PROVIDER resolves to Bedrock, flipped specifically to keep the consent promise true. Two files still say it lands on OpenAI. The finding is the stale comment.

rows.to: unset ⇒ bedrock — and says why in ten lines above it

under.why: An environment variable with a legal meaning. The comment names the four documents that would become false and the constant that must bump — so the next person to set it knows they are amending a disclosure, not tuning a model.

rows.to: "Since AI_PROVIDER is unset, both land on OpenAI" — stale, and wrong

rows.title: The comment, in full
rows.detail: Three of its four sentences are accurate. The fourth is the one a reader would act on.

under.why: A warning comment that is itself out of date — the most dangerous kind, because its ⚠ and its accurate caller list buy credibility for the one clause that is false. bedrockConfig.ts:22 resolves unset to Bedrock.

rows.title: Repeated in a second file
rows.detail: lib/ai/openaiClient.ts:5-8 carries the same claim, so a reader who checks one for corroboration finds the other.

rows.title: What a reader would conclude
rows.detail: That filer text already reaches a processor outside the consent — i.e. that the promise is broken. It is not: the default was flipped precisely to keep it true.

AUTHORED.title: Profile
AUTHORED.sub: The longest form, and the gate before any refund is shown
AUTHORED.detail: Collects legal identity and SSN/ITIN. Continue holds the flow until every income document has finished reading, because the next screen states a refund and a half-parsed one is worse than a slow one.

children.title: Payout Gate
children.sub: Check synchronously, await the save, then re-read the server

rows.title: Save the profile
rows.detail: POST /api/profile. On success the session draft is cleared — the backend is now the source of truth.

rows.title: Ask BEFORE awaiting
rows.detail: hasPendingIncomeExtractions() is synchronous. Asked after the await, the screen paints for one frame on every filing.

under.why: One microtask decides whether a loading screen is meaningful or noise. This is the entire reason a synchronous hasPending exists beside the promise-based settle — and "teaches them to ignore it" is the actual cost being avoided.

rows.title: Re-read the case file
rows.detail: An empty queue is ambiguous: 'all finished' and 'all destroyed by a reload' look identical from the client.

under.why: The client's own bookkeeping is treated as a liveness hint, never as truth. Because the persistence hop is client-side, a reload destroys the fetches and the evidence of them together — so only the server can tell the two apart.

rows.title: Refuse if documents are missing
rows.detail: The same shared rule the interview step uses, so the question and the answer cannot drift apart across two pages.

under.caption: one rule, asked on two different pages

rows.to: the question and the answer now live on different pages

under.why: The rationale for a shared module, stated as a consequence rather than a principle. Two copies would not fail loudly — they would disagree quietly, and the disagreement surfaces as a refund figure computed from documents that had not finished parsing.

rows.to: the names of the missing documents, not a boolean

under.why: Returning names rather than a boolean is what lets both callers say WHICH document is missing. Note the four 1099 variants collapse into one presence test — any one of them satisfies the requirement.

rows.title: Only now advance the stage
rows.detail: /api/profile deliberately writes stage 'profile'. Only /api/documents/payout writes 'payout', after the gate has passed.

under.why: The stage string is the RESUME coordinate, so writing it early would let a reload route around an in-memory gate entirely. Holding it at "profile" is what makes the gate survive process death.

children.sub: The request body is cast to a type, never parsed or validated

group.note: Checks that are made, and checks that are skipped.

rows.value: Validated in the form before Continue

AUTHORED.title: Tax Engine
AUTHORED.sub: One straight-line pass from W-2 box 1 to the number on line 34

group.note: The path, the formulas behind it, and the two tables it reads.

shape.unit: lines, one straight path, no branching

AUTHORED.detail: computeIncomeEngine is 563 lines of ordered assignments with no branching on filer type. Every dollar follows one path, each step naming its Form 1040-NR line.

children.title: Refund Path
children.sub: W-2 box 1 to the refund, in eight named engine steps
children.detail: The engine takes the case file and returns a result. Following a single wage dollar through it is the shortest way to understand the whole computation.

rows.title: Sum the W-2s
rows.detail: wagesGross is box 1 across every W-2; wagesWithheld is box 2. Both plain sums.

under.why: The engine's first three lines, and the shape of all 563: read a fact, name it, move on. The treaty lookup sits immediately beside the gross so the exemption is computed before anything downstream can use the wrong figure.

rows.title: Apply the treaty exemption
rows.detail: Three conditions must all hold: a rule exists, its time limit hasn't expired, and it carries no source restriction.

rows.to: findTreatyRuleForCountryName returned something for this country and year
exemptYearsUsed is within the treaty's own time limit

under.why: Three independent ways for a treaty to not apply, evaluated as one conjunction. Each term is a different kind of failure — no treaty at all, a treaty that has run out, and a treaty that only covers income from a particular source.

rows.to: some treaties only exempt income paid from abroad — those are excluded here

rows.title: Taxable wages
rows.detail: wagesTaxable = gross − exempt, unless a 1042-S already substantiated the exemption, in which case gross stands.

under.why: The ternary encodes a paperwork rule: when the employer already reported the exempt portion on a 1042-S, subtracting it again would double-count the exemption. Same dollar, two documents, one subtraction.

rows.title: Into the totals cascade
rows.detail: ECI → AGI → taxable income → tax → total tax → refund. Each line names its Form 1040-NR line in a trailing comment.

under.why: The tax form's own arithmetic, transcribed. The comments are line numbers because that is the specification — anyone checking this work is holding the paper form, and Math.max(0, …) is there because a deduction larger than income yields zero taxable income, never a negative.

rows.title: Total tax and the refund
rows.detail: totalTax adds the Schedule NEC tax; refundOrDue is withholding minus tax. Positive is a refund.

under.why: The last line of the whole engine, and the only number the filer cares about. The comment on line 33 is unusually careful: it enumerates the form's terms and states that the ones not modeled are zero — so a reader can check the omission rather than discover it.

rows.title: The filer
rows.detail: Indonesian F-1, 3rd exempt year, present 300 days. W-2 $3,500 (box 2 $200). Scholarship 1042-S $12,000. Interest $50. Dividends $500 ($75 withheld). One stock lot: sold $2,000, cost $1,000. Charity $500.

rows.label: Why this filer
rows.value: The fixture exercises every income type at once, with values chosen so no two lines share a number

rows.label: Every figure below
rows.value: Asserted by tests/golden/1040nr-scheduleOI.test.ts — none of it is computed here

rows.title: Wages: 3,500 − 2,000 = 1,500
rows.detail: Indonesia Art 19(1)(b)(iii) caps the wage exemption at $2,000/yr. min(3500, 2000) = 2000 exempt, so wagesTaxable = 1,500.

rows.title: Scholarship: 12,000 − 12,000 = 0
rows.detail: Art 19(1)(b)(ii) is uncapped and carries no source restriction, so exempt_amount is null → Infinity → min(12000, ∞) = 12,000 exempt. scholarshipTaxable = 0.

rows.title: ECI = 1,500 + 0 = 1,500
rows.detail: Adjustments are 0, so AGI is also 1,500.

rows.title: Deduction = 500 (itemized)
rows.detail: Indonesia is not India, so no standard deduction. SALT withheld is 0, charity is 500 → itemized = 500. taxableIncome = max(0, 1500 − 500) = 1,000.

rows.title: Income tax = 101, not 100
rows.detail: 1,000 is under 100k, so the Tax Table applies: the $1,000–$1,025 row's midpoint is $1,012.50, × 10% = $101.25, rounded to $101. Taxing 1,000 directly would have given 100.

under.why: The one-dollar difference between the table and the formula, pinned by a test. This is the assertion that would fail if someone 'simplified' taxForIncome into a direct bracket calculation.

rows.title: NEC tax = 75 + 300 = 375
rows.detail: Dividends 500 × 15% (Indonesia Art 11(2)) = 75. Capital gain 2,000 − 1,000 = 1,000 net; present 300 days ≥ 183 so it is taxable at the flat 30% → 300.

rows.title: Total tax = 101 + 375 = 476
rows.detail: The $50 of bank interest never enters: §871(i) exempts portfolio interest paid to a nonresident regardless of treaty.

rows.title: Withheld = 200 + 75 = 275
rows.detail: W-2 box 2 plus the 1099-DIV box 4. The FICA on this W-2 — boxes 4 and 6, $217.00 and $50.75 — is deliberately NOT in this total: it is recovered on Form 843, not on this return.

under.code: const ficaWithheldInError = sum(w2s.map((w2) => w2.box4 + w2.box6));
under.why: Social Security (box 4) and Medicare (box 6) summed together — the figure an F-1 in their exempt years should never have had withheld. It is surfaced as a finding and pointedly kept out of totalWithholding, because folding it into the refund would claim it on the wrong form.

rows.title: refundOrDue = 275 − 476 = −201
rows.detail: Negative, so the filer owes $201. The payout screen renders this same figure with the label "You owe" and never recomputes it.

under.why: One engine, one set of numbers. The screen is forbidden from doing arithmetic precisely so it cannot disagree with the form being mailed — and a test enforces the footing rather than trusting the rule.

children.title: Tax Table
children.sub: Below $100k the IRS uses a band lookup, not the bracket formula
children.detail: Under $100,000 the IRS publishes a table in $50 bands, and a band's tax is the bracket tax at its MIDPOINT. Applying the brackets directly gives a different, wrong number.

rows.title: Under $100k → find the band midpoint
rows.detail: Bands widen with income: $5 below $25, $25 up to $3,000, then $50 all the way to $100,000.

under.why: Floor to the band, then add half its width. The +12.5 and +25 are literally half of 25 and 50 — the midpoint of the band the income fell into, which is the figure the IRS taxed when it printed the table.

rows.title: Tax the midpoint, round to the dollar
rows.detail: bracketTax at the midpoint, then the IRS convention: 50-99 cents rounds up.

under.why: The whole rule in four lines: below $100k tax the band midpoint, at or above it tax the exact income. One ternary is the difference between matching the IRS's printed table and quietly disagreeing with it by a few dollars on every return.

rows.title: Verified against the printed table

group.note: Two unrelated Stage values that happen to share the same defect.

AUTHORED.detail: The Stage union declares "documents" and "review". No route writes either. Gating a feature on one of them already made a reviewer sample pack silently never render.

rows.title: Both are declared with a comment
rows.detail: "Stage 2 — upload + extraction" and "Stage 3+4+5 — findings, computation, summary". They read as a plan, not as dead code.

under.code:
export type Stage =
  | "eligibility" // Stage 0 — residency check
  | "profile" // Stage 1a — filer identity
  | "confirm" // Stage 0b — document-derived eligibility confirmation
  | "interview" // Stage 1b — situation questions
  | "documents" // Stage 2 — upload + extraction
  | "review" // Stage 3+4+5 — findings, computation, summary
  | "payout" // Stage 5b — refund/amount-owed result + how to receive or pay it
  | "file" // Stage 6 — PDF download + instructions
  | "blocked"; // routed out (not F-1, resident, etc.)
under.why: Every member carries a stage number, so the union reads as a complete map of the product. Two of those numbers were never built — and the comments are what make that invisible, because they describe intent as confidently as they describe what exists.

rows.title: What it cost once
rows.detail: A reviewer sample pack gated on one of these silently never rendered. No error, no empty state — the condition was simply never true.

rows.title: Why it survives
rows.detail: A union member with no writer is valid TypeScript. Only grepping writers against the union finds it, which is what surfaced it here.
